title: Avalanche vs. Kings Game 1: Key takeaways as Colorado begins quest for Stanley Cup
content:
DENVER — Artturi Lehkonen’s ice-breaking goal Sunday was far from the biggest of his career. The Finn has scored not one but two overtime goals to send his teams to the Stanley Cup Final — 2021 with Montreal and 2022 with Colorado — as well as the game-winning goal in the 2022 Stanley Cup clinching game. He added more heroics at the 2026 Olympics, sending Finland to the medal round with an overtime goal.

But his past highlights don’t take away from the importance of what he did in Colorado’s 2-1 Game 1 win, getting to a highly protected area of the ice and finding a crucial goal.

“That’s how he scores,” coach Jared Bednar said. “He has a knack for coming up with pucks.”

Colorado found themselves in a tense 0-0 game late in the second. Then Lehkonen did what he does best: score a big goal. Nathan MacKinnon flung a puck toward the net from an odd angle, and Anton Forsberg allowed a rebound. Lehkonen, never afraid to go to the hard areas of the ice, swept it into the net. He punched the air with excitement.

“Didn’t really feel like there was a ton of offense (before the goal), but I felt like we had done some good things forechecking-wise to get a little bit of O-zone time and try to get some point shots and screens,” Brock Nelson said. “Good battle by Lekky and definitely easier when you’re able to get out 1-0, get the crowd into it.”

The Kings are a stingy defensive team when at their best. The longer they had hung around, the more the heavily favored Avalanche would have had reason to worry. Lehkonen put an end to the potential concern. Colorado scored again early in the third and survived a late Kings goal to secure the win. Nazem Kadri interrupted a stretch pass in the final minutes that would’ve potentially led to an Adrian Kempe breakaway: an impactful play to help seal the win.

“I think that’s the kind of game you can expect playing the Kings,” Bednar said. “Our guys played the right way and got the job done tonight, and then we gotta go do it again.”

Here are more takeaways from Game 1.

Bednar started Scott Wedgewood in net for Game 1: an unsurprising development but a notable one nonetheless given the fairly even split between Wedgewood and Mackenzie Blackwood all year. Wedgewood rewarded his coach’s trust, making big saves on Adrian Kempe and Trevor Moore early and finishing with 24 saves in all.

“I thought he was fantastic,” Bednar said. “Did everything he needed to do. Obviously, bigger stakes, more emotion, but (he) played the exact same way that he’s been playing for us all year.”

Wedgewood (45 games played, 43 starts) and Blackwood (39 games played, 36 starts) teamed up to win the Jennings Trophy, given to the goalie or goalie tandem that allows the fewest goals in a season. Blackwood entered the season as the presumed starter but missed the first 12 games with a lower-body injury, then suffered a lower-body injury in January. He finished the year with a .904 save percentage.

Wedgewood had a .921 save percentage on the year — first in the league among goalies who played more than half their team’s games — and went 31-6-6. He had never started a playoff game before Sunday, though he’d come in in relief three times for Dallas in 2023 and once for Colorado last year. At 33, he became the eighth-oldest goalie in NHL history to make his first playoff start and the third-oldest to win it.

“Obviously, a long career to get to this point,” Wedgewood said. “First TV timeout, I was talking to (Blackwood). Just kind of felt the heart rate was a little high. But once we got going, it felt like a normal hockey game.”

In Forsberg, the Kings also used a goalie not expected to be their starter earlier this season. Down the stretch, Forsberg took the reins from Darcy Kuemper — Colorado’s goalie when it won the 2022 Stanley Cup — and he had a solid game with 28 saves. Neither of the Avalanche’s goals were soft.

“He’s been great for us down the stretch,” Kings defenseman Mikey Anderson said. “He’s made some huge saves when we need him to.”

No team is going to be able to fully contain the Avalanche’s firepower, but Los Angeles did a solid job limiting dangerous chances for much of the game. The Kings, though, could not capitalize on their own opportunities to swing the game in their favor.

Most notably, Drew Doughty missed a golden chance in the first period. Moore burst past a slipping Josh Manson and put a puck on Wedgewood, who made the save. That led to sustained Kings pressure, culminating in a loose puck skipping to Doughty in front of a partially vacated net. He backhanded it for what looked like a sure goal, but the puck grazed Wedgewood’s left post and moved out of danger.

Artemi Panarin — who needs to perform like an elite player if the Kings are going to have a chance — also failed to bury a chance in the second. He had an open net to aim at but couldn’t properly gather a puck that appeared to be bouncing. His shot missed. (Panarin, to his credit, scored the Kings’ lone goal of the game with a six-on-four shot through traffic late in the third.)

“We had a couple empty nets we missed,” said Kings coach D.J. Smith, who liked the way his team played overall. “I think we could be on the net more.”

Midway through the second period, Logan O’Connor wired a shot past Anton Forsberg for what would’ve been his first goal of an injury-shortened season. The celebratory horn started to blast, but the operator quickly cut it off as the referee signaled that the goal wouldn’t count. As the puck flew through the air, Jack Drury made contact with Forsberg, impeding him from making the save.

Bednar challenged the call. Drew Doughty bumped Drury during the play, which seemed to send him into Forsberg. After a review, though, the challenge was unsuccessful.

“I saw Doughty make contact,” Bednar said. “Disguised it pretty well, but (he) backs into him, knocks him off his edges, into the goalie and we shot it in the net. To me, I’d like to see it count. They saw it different. I’m not losing any sleep over it. Kill the penalty and move on.”

Colorado successfully killed off the penalty; O’Connor thought the penalty kill unit “did a good job just to stunt the momentum that could’ve provided our team after we didn’t get that one (overturned).”

Goaltending interference has been a frequent cause of confusion for teams this season, so much so that it became a topic of conversation at the annual general managers meetings in March. Commissioner Gary Bettman defended the review process at the meetings, saying “if you look at the body of work, I think our video replay system not only has been a leader among the sports (leagues) because all the other systems are modeled on ours.”

O’Connor got his revenge for the waved-off goal. Just under six minutes into the third, he used his elite speed to pick up a loose puck in the offensive zone and cut to the net. With a step on Cody Ceci, he wristed a shot over Forsberg’s glove.

O’Connor had offseason hip surgery last summer and went goalless in the 13 regular season games he played, adding to the excitement around his goal.

“The guy just shows up and works extremely hard,” Brock Nelson said. “For him to get rewarded was nice. I think it’s been a long time coming.”

On paper, the Avalanche should have an elite power play. For much of the year, that wasn’t the case. It finished the season ranked 27th with a 17.1 percent conversion rate. The unit improved later in the season, ranking 16th after the Olympic break (21.4 percent), but it didn’t have a good Game 1 against the Kings, who had the league’s third-worst kill in the regular season. The unit went 0-for-4.

Colorado’s top power-play grouping failed to get settled enough for any dangerous looks during its first opportunity. Its second try produced dangerous looks but couldn’t beat Forsberg, then the third ended prematurely after a Martin Nečas holding penalty.

Late in the third period, after the Kings drew within a goal, Colorado got its final power play when Joel Armia high-sticked Josh Manson. That power play did its job — it made sure the Kings didn’t tie the game before the final horn — but also missed on chances to score. Nečas hit a post, and Colorado couldn’t ice the game when Los Angeles killed Forsberg to shift play to five-on-five.

One game isn’t reason to panic for Colorado. But if it’s going to make a deep run, it will need the power play to perform more like it did in the final stretch of the season than it did at the beginning.

• MacKinnon and Nečas played mostly with Lehkonen on their left wing, but Bednar replaced Lehkonen at points with Nelson, Kadri and Gabriel Landeskog. He did so for left-side faceoffs, which Nelson, Kadri and Landeskog are better at than MacKinnon, the line’s center. The coach wanted to maximize possession time.

• After his team’s loss, Smith said he probably would’ve taken a 1-0 deficit after two periods. The Kings were in position to tie the game with one shot. Overall, he saw “a lot of good things” in the way his team played. Natural Stat Trick said the Kings had 56.97 percent of the expected goal share at five-on-five.

• Before Sunday, Panarin’s most recent playoff game was the Rangers’ Game 6 loss to the Panthers in the 2024 Eastern Conference final. Both that game and Sunday ended with Panarin’s team losing 2-1 after he scored a goal with his goalie pulled in the final minutes.
